items.summary:

One mom’s viral video hit a nerve 

Grady can be seen looking out the window of her home at her Boomer mom and dad carrying bags and boxes up her driveway after several visits. The distressed and contemplative look on Grady’s face is speaking to plenty of Millennial moms.

Grady captioned the video, “Today’s ‘treasure’ highlight was the mobile that hung in my nursery…”

items.t: Millennial parents are pleading with Boomer grandparents to stop giving excessive gifts to grandkids

items.title: Woman featured in iconic Great Depression photo didn’t know she was famous until 40 years later
items.summary:
It’s one of the most iconic and haunting photos of all time, up there with the likes of Hindenburg, The Falling Soldier , Burning Monk, Napalm Girl , and many others. It’s called simply Migrant Mother , and it paints a better picture of the time in which it was taken than any book or interview possibly could.

Nearly everyone across the globe knows Florence Owens Thompson’s face from newspapers, magazines, and history books. The young, destitute mother was the face of the Great Depression , her worried, suntanned face looking absolutely defeated as several of her children took comfort by resting on her thin frame. Thompson put a human face and emotion behind the very real struggle of the era, but she wasn’t even aware of her role in helping to bring awareness to the effects of the Great Depression on families.

It turns out that Dorothea Lange, the photographer responsible for capturing the worry-stricken mother in the now-famous photo, told Thompson that the photos wouldn’t be published.

An iconic photograph of Florence Owens Thompson with her children during the Great Depression. Photo credit: Dorothea Lange/Wikipedia 

Of course, they subsequently were published in the San Francisco News . At the time the photo was taken, Thompson was supposedly only taking respite at the migrant campsite with her seven children after the family car broke down near the campsite. The photo was taken in March 1936 in Nipomo, California when Lange was concluding a monthlong photography excursion documenting migrant farm labor.

What life was really like for Thompson

items.t: Woman featured in iconic Great Depression photo didn’t know she was famous until 40 years later

items.title: Beavers were brought to the desert to save a dying river. 6 years later, here are the results.
items.summary:
It’s not easy being a river in the desert under the best of circumstances. The ecosystem exists in a very delicate balance, allowing water sources to thrive in the harsh conditions. These water sources in otherwise extremely dry areas are vital to the survival of unique wildlife, agriculture, and even tourism as they provide fresh drinking water for the people who live nearby.

But man-made problems like climate change, over-farming, and pollution have made a tough job even tougher in some areas. Rivers in Utah and Colorado that are part of the Colorado River Basin have been barely surviving the extremely harsh drought season. When the riverbeds get too dry, fish and other aquatic creatures die off and the wildfire risk increases dramatically.

A bold idea to save a desert river 

About seven years ago, one team of researchers had a fascinating idea to restore the health of some of Utah’s most vulnerable rivers: Bring in the beavers.

Beaver in water. Photo credit: Svetozar Cenisev/Unsplash 

In 2019, master’s student Emma Doden and a team of researchers from Utah State University began a “translocation” project to bring displaced beavers to areas like Utah’s Price River, in the hopes of bringing it back to life.

Why beavers? It just makes dam sense! (Sorry.)

Beaver dams restrict the flow of water in some areas of a river, creating ponds and wetlands. In drought-stricken areas, fish and other wildlife can take refuge in the ponds while the rest of the river runs dry, thus riding out the danger until it rains again.

When beavers are present in a watershed, the benefits…
items.t: Beavers were brought to the desert to save a dying river. 6 years later, here are the results.

items.title: A confidence expert shares a simple body language gesture that signals if a person is trustworthy and confident
items.summary:
Confidence is not always easy to have in social settings, especially when meeting new people . In 2021, a YouGov study found that 37% of Americans reported feeling “not very confident” in new social groups.

But there may be a simple gesture that can help you appear more confident . During an episode of communication expert Jefferson Fisher’s podcast, he sat down with Dr. Shadé Zahrai, PhD, a confidence expert and co-author of Big Trust: Rewire Self-Doubt, Find Your Confidence, and Fuel Success . Dr. Zahrai shared a body language gesture that can help indicate if a person is confident or not.

She explains the tell-tale sign is in the upper body. “The distance between the chin and your chest,” she tells Fisher.

View this post on Instagram 

What confident body language looks like 

Dr. Zahrai explains why the distance between the chest and chin can indicate confidence.

“When you’re slouching, when you’re withdrawing, when you feel insecure, yeah sure shoulders go… but it’s also your head that drops,” she says, gesturing her head to tilt downwards. “So if you can just think, ‘Okay, what is the distance between my chin and my chest, and how do I elongate it? Not by looking at the ceiling, but in a natural state, you will naturally feel more empowered.’“

Dr. Zahrai suggests that this also builds a sense of trustworthiness between others that will encourage connection .

“And you will naturally convey more of that big trust energy that we’re seeking,” she adds. “The idea is when you’re showing up as the person you want to be, people then respond to that.”

She notes that it…
items.t: A confidence expert shares a simple body language gesture that signals if a person is trustworthy and confident

items.title: The fascinating reason people looked much older in the past than they do today
items.summary:
Ever look at your parents’ high school yearbooks and think people looked so much older back then? All of the teenagers look like they’re in their mid-30s and the teachers who are 50 look like they’re 80. When we watch older movies, even those from the 1980s , the teenagers appear to be a lot older as well. Why is it that they looked so much older ? Was life harder? Did people act more mature? Did they spend more time outdoors and less time playing video games? Is it their sense of fashion? Were they all smokers?

Educator Michael Stevens , who runs the super-popular Vsauce YouTube channel, explains the phenomenon in a video called, “Did people used to look older?” In it, he explains that people in the past appear a lot older due to retrospective aging.

What is retrospective aging? 

This is how it works: when we see people in the past, they are wearing outdated styles that we associate with older people; therefore, we think they have aged rapidly. For example, a teenager in the 1950s may have been in fashion while wearing thick Buddy Holly-style glasses .

Buddy Holly was 20 years old in this photo. Photo credit: Wikimedia Commons 

But as people age, they tend to cling to the fashion of their youth . So many people of that generation continued to wear the Buddy Holly-style glasses into their 50s. So when younger people see those glasses they see them as old people’s glasses and not a hip kid from the ’50s.

So in the photo from the ’50s, the teen appears to look a lot older because our perspective has been tainted by time.

But it isn’t all just an illusion. Stevens also…
items.t: The fascinating reason people looked much older in the past than they do today

items.title: In 1997, Blur recorded a 2-minute song to prank their record label. It became a ’90s anthem.
items.summary:
“Song 2” by Blur has been a mainstay at sporting events and in action movies for nearly 30 years, with its blazing guitars, iconic drum intro, and irresistibly simple “Woo-hoo” chorus. Although Blur had a knack for writing incredibly catchy tunes , most of their music, up to 1997, was Indie rock that leaned into social commentary on modern British life . Not the kinda stuff you’d hear over a loudspeaker at a Dallas Cowboys game.

By 1997, the band was moving away from Britpop, a genre it helped define, which celebrated an over-the-top, cartoony Britishness, sneered at the Americanization of UK culture, and stood in opposition to grunge rock. When the band hit the studio to record its 5th album, the eponymous Blur , they did an about-face. The band began taking cues from its former enemies across the pond, embracing American noise rock and hip-hop.

Blur’s ‘Song 2’ began very differently 

Damon Albarn, the band’s singer and primary songwriter, brought a goofy song to one of their sessions: an acoustic bossa nova with a chorus that had a whistle like a cat-call or, as they say in the UK, a “wolf whistle.” 

Here’s what the original “Song 2” sounded like:

When Blur’s guitarist Graham Coxon heard the song, he told Albarn , “That’s too f***ing nice,” and proposed something entirely different. “I was like, ‘Let’s do it really fast, really noisy, and really horrible, and tell the record label we want to record it as a single. It’ll scare them to death. They’ll hate it,'” Coxon told Produce Like a Pro . 

The band rearranged the song with a quiet verse and an extremely loud…
items.t: In 1997, Blur recorded a 2-minute song to prank their record label. It became a ’90s anthem.

items.title: People swear these 15 psychological ‘cheat codes’ improve how you’re treated in social situations
items.summary:
The funny thing about social intelligence is that it’s a major factor in how successful we are in relationships, careers, and managing our mental health. We shape children’s behavior to follow social norms, but most parents don’t teach them how to make small talk, handle rude people, or how long to hold eye contact.

Many assume these communication habits are innate, but people with great communication and interpersonal skills aren’t just born that way; they often hone their skills like an athlete or musician. The good news is that almost anyone can improve their communication skills with a little practice.

A man giving a speech. Credit: Canva 

Recently, a Redditor asked people on the Answers forum to share the tricks they use in social situations. “What is a social ‘cheat code’ that completely changes how people treat you?” they asked, and they received nearly 1,000 responses; many shared good advice on handling rude people or improving their likability. 

Here are 15 of the best social ‘cheat codes’ in the thread.

1. Let them think they’re smart 

“People are easier to manipulate if you let them believe that they’re smarter than you.” 

“Ahh, yes, the Columbo Method.” 

2. Lose weight 

“The difference in how people treat you when you’re thin vs fat is astounding. When I first lost weight around 22, it caused me a lot of anger & resentment because of the huge difference in attitudes & attraction people suddenly had towards me. When I got older & put weight back on, I also noticed how I slowly became invisible again & people treated it like an inconvenience if they had…
items.t: People swear these 15 psychological ‘cheat codes’ improve how you’re treated in social situations

items.title: He lost his job and started mowing lawns for free. Now 2,100 volunteers have joined him.
items.summary:
When Brian Schwartz got laid off in 2020, right in the thick of the COVID-19 pandemic , everything was upside down. In addition to losing his job, he was a new father who was also caring for a sick parent. On top of that, the whole world felt uncertain and unmoored in a way none of us had ever experienced.

One could sit at home and wallow in such circumstances. But Schwartz took another tack; he looked outside of himself to see where he could help someone else. He noticed some elderly neighbors needed help with their yards and figured that was a safe, socially distanced way to offer some service.

Now, that single idea has blossomed into a full-fledged, award-winning network of 2,100 volunteers. Neighbors helping neighbors, in every state in the nation. And it’s still growing.

On Day 4 of #HOPEWeek , we recognized Brian Schwartz and his national non-profit, "I Want To Mow Your Lawn" 

Originated during the pandemic, @IWTMYL provides older adults, veterans, and neighbors facing physical or financial hardship with free, temporary lawn care relief… pic.twitter.com/1aQkHG822X

items.title: A 10-year-old boy’s liver saved her life when she was a baby. She just married his little brother.
items.summary:
In December 2003, two families in neighboring states were living through opposite nightmares . In Kentucky, 18-month-old Brooklyn Dotson was dying. A rare liver condition had left her days from death without a transplant, and in Ohio, 10-year-old Michael Waters had just been struck and killed by a car .

Michael had told his family he wanted to be an organ donor, and they honored that wish. His liver went to Brooklyn, who received the transplant at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital.

“Even as a kid, he’d do anything for anybody,” his younger brother, Noah Waters, told LEX 18 . “He was a sweet kid. Probably he was way more mature than he needed to be.”

The two families met in person in 2005 and stayed in touch over the years. Brooklyn and Noah, who was five years younger than his late brother, became close friends. He was there for her when she needed another surgery as a teenager.

Then, in 2025, things shifted. Brooklyn realized her feelings for Noah had changed, and her mom let him know. That weekend, he drove from Ohio to Kentucky to tell her he had always felt the same way.

“It got to the point we were FaceTiming each other 8 hours a day,” Brooklyn said.

Noah proposed on Christmas Eve. On Sept. 26, they were married overlooking Lake Cumberland in Kentucky, and Brooklyn took the Waters name.

“I was crying all day,” Noah told People . He believes his brother was looking out for him from heaven.

He’s also clear-eyed about how unusual their path was. “I’d say he probably knew what his purpose was,” he told LEX 18. “I had no idea that my brother was gonna save my wife’s…
items.t: A 10-year-old boy’s liver saved her life when she was a baby. She just married his little brother.

items.title: Peacock breaks into couple’s house just to look in the mirror. Then he leads entire neighborhood on a weeklong chase.
items.summary:
Geoff and Delwyn Ballantyne only stepped out for an evening coffee . When they returned to their home in Alexandra Hills, a suburb of Brisbane, Australia, a male peacock was in their bathroom, gazing at himself in the vanity mirror .

“There was a lot of screaming from my wife,” Geoff told The Guardian . “She thought there must have been an intruder, but then she says it’s a peacock. I did believe her, but I tried not to, because it wasn’t very believable.”

They tried to tempt him away with water and crackers, but he wouldn’t leave the mirror. Wildlife rescuers eventually wrapped him in a towel and released him into nearby bushland.

But he didn’t stay there. The peacock started showing up every afternoon at the acreage property of another Alexandra Hills resident, Suzie Tafolo, who suspected he belonged to a local tattoo artist, Elliot Ross. Ross had been searching for his missing peacock, Hex, and confirmed from photos that the bathroom intruder was him.

Then Tafolo did some research. “I’ve Googled how to catch a peacock, which is something I never thought I’d have to do,” she said. “One of the things it says is that they love mirrors, which makes sense in terms of how he ended up in the bathroom.”

So she hauled a full-length mirror out to the shed where Hex kept turning up.

The mirror probably wasn’t about vanity. Urban ecologist Darryl Jones told The Guardian that most birds read their reflection as another bird, and Hex may simply have been drawn to what looked like company. Ross had his own theory. “We’ve got a female here as well, and she’s stayed,” he said.…
items.t: Peacock breaks into couple’s house just to look in the mirror. Then he leads entire neighborhood on a weeklong chase.

items.title: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
items.summary:
This story has been co-published by  Reasons to be Cheerful  and the  Outrider Foundation . 

I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.”  

The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” 

He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.”  

Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth 
 Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by:   

never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy 

Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to…
items.t: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future

items.title: What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives
items.summary:
Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. 

In the bag 
 A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. 

“The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” 

Michaela says: 
 I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. 

Bird’s-eye view 

In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds.

items.t: What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives
